source_links.title: Post-tsunami resettlement in Sri Lanka and India: site planning, infrastructure and services

text:
Case study: Chennai (Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India)
Section: CASE STUDY OVERVIEW

**Case Name and Location:** Post-Tsunami Resettlement of Coastal Fishing Communities, Coromandel Coast, Tamil Nadu, India. Primary case sites are nine fishing villages located along the Coromandel Coast in Thiruvallur, Kanchipuram, Villupuram, and Nagapattinam districts of Tamil Nadu, plus the Srinivasapuram neighbourhood of Chennai, Tamil Nadu. Comparative case sites are Hambantota New Town, Hambantota town, and Seenigama in Southern Sri Lanka. Note: The Sri Lanka and India programmes operated under distinct regulatory frameworks and are treated as related but separate contexts throughout this document.

**Hazard(s):** The Indian Ocean Tsunami of 26 December 2004.

**Type of Retreat:** Community-level resettlement — the relocation of entire or partial fishing settlements to newly constructed inland housing. In Tamil Nadu, this was implemented through a public–private partnership in which state government provided land and NGOs constructed standardized housing. In Sri Lanka, a post-tsunami buffer zone policy restricting rebuilding along the coast led to plans for new settlements on land outside the buffer zone, funded by international and local NGOs and philanthropic organizations, with land donated by government or purchased by NGOs. In Chennai (Srinivasapuram), the government proposed relocating fishing families approximately 22 km away, but strong community resistance delayed any permanent construction.

**Scale:** Across Tamil Nadu, the Tsunami Rehabilitation Programme proposed the construction of 84,542 houses (government: 47,491; NGO: 37,051); approximately 45,035 were completed. The paper by Bavinck et al. (2015) reports 686,069 hectares of housing land acquired, though the table note indicates this figure does not distinguish government- and NGO-procured land. The nine Coromandel Coast case study villages varied widely in size, from small hamlets to larger fishing settlements; Akkaraipettai, the largest site, saw approximately 768 houses constructed by the Tata Relief Committee for some 3,500 people, while the smallest studied site (Nemmeli Kuppam) comprised 42 houses. In Srinivasapuram, Chennai, according to a survey of the Tamil Nadu Slum Clearance Board (TNSCB), 769 families out of a total of 3,086 families in the area belonged to the fishing community; 54 people died in the tsunami. In Sri Lanka, more than a million people were affected overall, nearly 90,000 houses were completely or partially damaged, and plans were made to build 43,000 new houses on 387 sites outside the buffer zone; Hambantota New Town alone comprised 2,330 houses.

**Key Actors:**
- *Tamil Nadu (Coromandel Coast sites)*: Government of Tamil Nadu (district authorities, Revenue Administration, Disaster Management and Mitigation Department) provided land and issued GO 172 (March 2005) and CRZ-based guidelines. Different NGOs were responsible for construction at each site: Madras Social Society Service (MSSS) in Sathankuppam; Evangelical Church of India (ECI) and Government in Karikattukuppam; Village Community Development Society (VCDS) and World Vision in Mandavai Pudukuppam; Joyce Meyer Ministries (JMM) and YMCA Salem in Koonimedu Kuppam; Lutheran World Service (LWS) and Billy Graham Evangelical Association (BGEA) in Anichan Kuppam; Amma Foundation/Trust in Samanthaipettai; Tata Relief Committee (TRC) in Akkaraipettai; World Vision in Kallar. Caste panchayats played an important intermediary role in several sites.
- *Chennai (Srinivasapuram)*: Tamil Nadu Slum Clearance Board (TNSCB) was the agency responsible for tsunami housing reconstruction. UNTRS (United Nations Team for Recovery Support), mentioned in Raju (2013) as a UN coordination body for tsunami recovery activities in Tamil Nadu, was among stakeholders interviewed. NGOs operating in the field opposed the proposed relocation.
- *Sri Lanka*: Various international and local NGOs, philanthropic, political and religious organizations implemented housing in Hambantota New Town (on government-donated land); a local NGO implemented programmes in Seenigama (on privately purchased land). The research on Sri Lanka and Chennai was supported by Australian Research Council (ARC) funding and further informed by an AusAID-funded study.

**Timeline:** Tsunami: 26 December 2004. Emergency relief and initial planning: January–March 2005. Government of Tamil Nadu GO 172 issued: 30 March 2005. Construction of new settlements underway in most Tamil Nadu sites: 2005–2007, with some sites (e.g., Karikattukuppam) still under construction as of 2008–2010. The fastest completion was Samanthaipettai, where residents received keys before Christmas 2005, approximately six months after the tsunami. Field research by Bavinck et al.: April–June 2008. Data collection for the Raju (2013) study in Srinivasapuram: May 2008. As of May 2008, four years after the tsunami, the Chennai community and state were still debating and negotiating relocation, and no permanent housing had been constructed for Srinivasapuram residents.

**Key Outcomes:** Approximately 45,035 houses were completed across Tamil Nadu under the programme. Many fisher households expressed satisfaction with the physical quality of new concrete houses compared to earlier thatch or self-built structures, and with basic infrastructure improvements (electricity, water, connecting roads) in some sites. However, the distance of new settlements from the shoreline was widely perceived as impairing fishing livelihoods — an impediment to monitoring sea conditions, launching boats, drying nets, and storing equipment. In several sites (notably Samanthaipettai), some households moved back to the old settlement or maintained partial residence in both locations. In Kallar, where the new settlement was built six kilometres inland, fishers faced severe livelihood disruption; women who relocated to New Kallar generally lost income-generating opportunities they had previously held in fisheries. Community participation in house design and allocation was limited in most sites. Random allocation of houses disrupted existing social ties in some communities. In Srinivasapuram, Chennai, community resistance delayed housing reconstruction significantly; as of the research period (2008), no permanent housing had been built and residents were living in damaged buildings or self-constructed temporary shelters. In Sri Lanka, infrastructure deficiencies (drainage, water supply, sanitation, transport, security) were common in new settlements, and some beneficiaries had abandoned, leased, or transferred their properties.

**Narrative Summary:**

When the Indian Ocean Tsunami struck on 26 December 2004, it devastated fishing communities across Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka, destroying houses, boats, and equipment and killing thousands. The Tamil Nadu state government and a wide array of NGOs responded by constructing new housing settlements inland, using the Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) 1991 Notification — originally an environmental protection instrument — as the legal basis for relocating communities away from the coast. Government Order 172 of March 2005 guided this process, recommending that new settlements be located at least 500 metres from the High Tide Line. By the time of the primary research fieldwork in 2008, over 45,000 houses had been completed under the Tamil Nadu programme, and Sri Lanka had embarked on plans for 43,000 new houses on 387 sites outside its post-tsunami buffer zone.

However, outcomes across the studied sites reveal a persistent gap between the safety rationale advanced by the state and the livelihood realities of fishing communities. Fisher households depend on proximity to the sea for their economic survival — to monitor weather and sea conditions, launch boats, dry and store nets and gear, and sell or process fish along the shoreline. Relocating settlements hundreds of metres or even kilometres from the shore disrupted these practices substantially. In several Tamil Nadu sites, families moved back to the old coastal location, maintained dual residences, or rented out their new houses rather than occupying them. In Kallar, where authorities placed the new settlement six kilometres inland, fishers faced the most extreme livelihood disruption; women who relocated lost income-generating opportunities in fisheries. In Srinivasapuram, Chennai, the community's organized resistance to a proposed relocation 22 kilometres away blocked the process entirely, leaving residents in damaged or temporary structures four years after the disaster.

The planning process was broadly characterized by top-down decision-making, limited community consultation, and standardized house designs imposed without reference to fishing household needs. Infrastructure provision was frequently inadequate or delayed in both India and Sri Lanka — drainage, water supply, sanitation, and transport links all presented serious problems in many new settlements. Where caste panchayats were cohesive and widely recognized, as in Sathankuppam and Anichan Kuppam, communities fared better in negotiating outcomes; where panchayat legitimacy was contested, as in Koonimedu Kuppam, the process was delayed and less satisfactory. Critics, including NGO representatives interviewed in Chennai, argued that the tsunami was used as a trigger to relocate fishing communities from the coast on the pretext of safety — a view echoed in academic commentary linking the process to "disaster capitalism." Questions about the future of coastal land rights and the sustainability of relocated communities remained unresolved as of the research period.

---

text:
Case study: Chennai (Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India)
Section: CODING QUESTIONS

---

### Is there any evidence of a proactive or reactive trigger in the MR decision process? (Reactive/Proactive)

**Answer:** **Reactive** (primary coding), with a proactive framing applied post-hoc by state authorities.

**Narrative:** The relocation decisions across all studied sites were fundamentally triggered by the catastrophic Indian Ocean Tsunami of 26 December 2004 — a reactive response to an already-occurred disaster. The Tamil Nadu state government's GO 172 (30 March 2005) and the broader Tsunami Rehabilitation Programme were explicitly post-disaster responses. In Sri Lanka, the buffer zone policy was enacted in the immediate aftermath of the tsunami. This is clearly reactive in character.

However, state actors framed the relocation as contributing to proactive risk reduction for future coastal hazards. Bavinck et al. (2015, p. 592) note that "the tsunami was considered in the context of an ongoing string of natural hazards affecting the coastline, which, along with climate change, are expected to worsen," and that policymakers "underlined the opportunity to relocate human settlements in the interior, helping to safeguard populations from future threats." The pre-existing CRZ 1991 Notification provided a pre-established regulatory framework that was reinterpreted to justify the setback-based relocation.

Raju (2013) records that respondents from fishing communities and NGOs "explain that the tsunami has been used as a trigger to relocate these communities away from the coast on the pretext of disaster recovery and safety," suggesting the disaster was treated as an opportunity for relocation rather than purely as a safety imperative.

**Coding rationale:** **Reactive** is the appropriate primary code. The proactive framing was applied by state authorities after the disaster occurred, using a pre-existing regulatory instrument (CRZ 1991) that was not designed for post-disaster resettlement. It does not represent pre-event proactive planning.

---

### Date, Number of households affected, Number of population affected, Total funding

**Answer:**

- **Date:** Tsunami: 26 December 2004. Programme commencement: early 2005. GO 172 issued: 30 March 2005. Construction substantially underway: 2005–2007. Some sites still under construction as of 2008–2010. Chennai still in negotiation as of May 2008.

- **Number of households affected (Tamil Nadu programme):** 84,542 houses proposed (government: 47,491; NGO: 37,051); approximately 45,035 completed as of the research period (Bavinck et al., 2015, Table 2). At the nine Coromandel Coast study sites, individual projects ranged from 42 houses (Nemmeli Kuppam) to 768 houses (Akkaraipettai). In Srinivasapuram, Chennai, 769 fishing families out of 3,086 total families in the area were identified by the TNSCB survey (Raju, 2013).

- **Number of population affected (Tamil Nadu):** The total fishing population on the Coromandel Coast was estimated at 296,116 (Central Marine Fisheries Research Institute, 2005, cited in Bavinck et al., 2015). Losses of life in Tamil Nadu totalled 8,009 (Table 1, Bavinck et al., 2015); the Coromandel Coast-specific figure is not separately reported in the source. In Srinivasapuram, 54 people died in the tsunami (Raju, 2013). Akkaraipettai experienced approximately 700 deaths (Bavinck et al., 2015, p. 603).

- **Number of households and population affected (Sri Lanka):** More than a million people were affected; more than 35,000 killed; nearly 90,000 houses completely or partially damaged. Plans were made for 43,000 new houses on 387 sites. Hambantota New Town: 2,330 houses; Hambantota town apartment scheme: 40 households; Seenigama Case 1: 84 households; Seenigama Case 2: 50 households; Chennai Case 1: 960 households; Chennai Case 2: 432 households (Ahmed & McEvoy, 2014, Table I).

- **Total funding:** No aggregate programme-level funding figure is provided in the reviewed sources. The Tamil Nadu programme was a public–private partnership with state government providing land and NGOs providing construction funding. Sri Lankan reconstruction was funded by international NGOs, philanthropic organizations, and government (land donation). The Ahmed & McEvoy (2014) research was funded by the Australian Research Council (ARC) and an AusAID-funded study (Shaw and Ahmed, 2010). Raju (2013) states the author received no funding for the research.

**Uncertainty:** Total programme funding figures are not reported in the sources reviewed. Individual site funding arrangements varied by NGO and by site.

---

### What is the occurrence of the hazard(s) considered in the MR decision process? (Single Hazard/Multiple Hazards)

**Answer:** **Single Hazard** (tsunami as the immediate decision trigger).

**Narrative:** The direct trigger for the managed retreat decisions was the 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami — a single catastrophic event. However, Bavinck et al. (2015, p. 592) note that authorities framed the tsunami "in the context of an ongoing string of natural hazards affecting the coastline, which, along with climate change, are expected to worsen." The CRZ 1991 Notification — the legal framework used to justify the setback — was originally designed for broader coastal zone environmental protection, not specifically for tsunamis. The Coromandel Coast is also affected by cyclonic storms from the Bay of Bengal (Bavinck et al., 2015, p. 593).

**Coding rationale:** The MR decision was triggered by a single hazard event (the tsunami). The broader coastal hazard framing was contextual justification rather than a separate, independent driver of the retreat decision. **Single Hazard** is the appropriate primary code; the broader coastal risk framing is noted as contextual background.

---

### What is the origin of the hazards considered in the MR decision process? (Technological Hazard/Natural Hazard)

**Answer:** **Natural Hazard.**

**Narrative:** The Indian Ocean Tsunami of 2004 was a naturally occurring seismic and oceanographic event. There is no evidence in the reviewed sources of any technological or industrial component to the hazard. The broader coastal hazards referenced in the CRZ framework (cyclones, storm surges, coastal erosion) are also natural hazards.

**Coding:** **Natural Hazard.**

---

### Was this hazard considered in the MR decision process? (Coastal Flooding/Erosion), (Riverine/Pluvial Flooding), (Lake Flooding/Erosion), (Wildfire), (Volcano), (Land Subsidence), (Landslide/Debris Flow), (Earthquake), (Tsunami), (Hurricane), (Other)

**Answer:** **Tsunami** (primary and direct decision trigger).

**Narrative:** The tsunami was the direct and explicit driver of the retreat decision in all studied sites. Bavinck et al. (2015) and Raju (2013) both confirm the tsunami as the triggering event. The CRZ 1991 regulatory framework and GO 172 were applied in the tsunami recovery context.

As secondary contextual background: Bavinck et al. (2015, p. 593) mention that "cyclonic storms that develop in the open expanse of the Bay of Bengal beat the shoreline at great velocity, a few times a year on occasion," situating the tsunami within a broader coastal hazard environment. However, cyclones or other coastal hazards were not independent triggers for the retreat decision — they were cited by state actors to justify the broader policy rationale.

**Coding:** **Tsunami** (primary, direct). Broader coastal hazard context noted but not coded as an independent decision trigger.

---

### What was the geographic scale of the MR project? (Individual homes), (A few streets), (Neighbourhood), (Entire community), (Sub-watershed), (Watershed region)

**Answer:** **Entire Community** (stated government intent in most sites); **Neighbourhood** (actual outcome in several sites, and in the Chennai urban context).

**Narrative:** In most Coromandel Coast case study sites, the government aimed to relocate the entire fishing community. For example, in Kallar, "government directives prescribe the movement of the entire population of Kallar" (Bavinck et al., 2015, p. 604). In Sathankuppam, "a majority of the villagers agreed to resettle" collectively. In Akkaraipettai, 768 houses were built for "some 3,500 people from Akkaraipettai."

In practice, several villages experienced partial relocation — some families moved to new sites while others remained in or returned to original locations — producing neighbourhood-scale rather than full community-scale outcomes. In Mandavai Pudukuppam, "some families have chosen to stay in their old houses." In Koonimedu Kuppam, "a section of the village population has continued to live in old quarters."

In Srinivasapuram, Chennai, the proposed relocation encompassed 769 fishing families within a specific urban neighbourhood. In Sri Lanka, Hambantota New Town (2,330 houses) effectively represented a new community-scale settlement.

**Coding:** **Entire Community** (stated intent in most Tamil Nadu sites); **Neighbourhood** (actual outcome where partial relocation occurred, and appropriate scale for Srinivasapuram and some Sri Lanka urban schemes).

---

### Who or what was retreated? (Individuals), (Groups/Neighbourhoods), (Communities), (Critical infrastructure), (Hazard protection structures), (Industrial assets)

**Answer:** **Communities** (primary stated intent); **Groups/Neighbourhoods** (actual outcome in several sites).

**Narrative:** The retreat primarily involved fishing communities as collective units — entire villages or urban neighbourhood settlements. Panchayat-level collective decision-making (e.g., Sathankuppam), government directives for entire village relocation (Kallar), and the construction of collective settlement sites all point to community-level retreat as the design intent. In practice, social differentiation within communities meant that different households responded differently (e.g., in Akkaraipettai, trawler crew members were most likely to move to the new settlement, while boat owners and small-scale fishers tended to stay in the old neighbourhood). This produced group- and neighbourhood-level outcomes rather than uniform community-wide retreat.

No evidence of infrastructure-only managed realignment, hazard protection structure relocation, or industrial asset retreat is present in the reviewed sources.

**Coding:** **Communities** (primary intent); **Groups/Neighbourhoods** (actual outcome in many sites).

---

### Other notes

The case involves a complex interplay between post-disaster humanitarian response and pre-existing coastal zone regulatory policy. The CRZ 1991 Notification was designed for environmental protection but was reinterpreted to justify resettlement setbacks. Its application to post-tsunami recovery created significant ambiguities resolved inconsistently by district authorities. The role of caste panchayats as informal governance structures is a distinctive feature of the Tamil Nadu context documented in Bavinck et al. (2015).

---

text:
Case study: Chennai (Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India)
Section: INSTITUTIONAL ENVIRONMENT

---

### What is the focus or scope of the MR project? (Individual buyout/retreat), (Community buyout/retreat), (Leasebacks, easements and buffers), (Other acquisition tools), (Managed realignment of infrastructure)

**Answer:** **Community buyout/retreat** (used here to mean collective community relocation, not a financial property buyout); **Other acquisition tools** (government land provision and NGO-funded construction as the operative mechanism).

**Narrative:** The retreat involved collective relocation of fishing communities to newly constructed settlements, not individual property buyouts. There was no market-value compensation or property purchase from existing owners. Most fisher households lived on government-owned wasteland (poromboke) and had no formal title to their land. The state government provided land and NGOs funded construction; this is described by Bavinck et al. (2015, p. 596) as "a public–private venture, with government seeking the collaboration of NGOs. The general pattern therein seems to have been that the former provided the land (either from its own reserves or, in rare instances, procuring it from private owners), while the latter contributed to the construction process."

In Sri Lanka, the buffer zone policy restricted rebuilding along the coast. New settlements were built on government-donated land (Hambantota New Town) or private land purchased by NGOs (Seenigama). Houses were allocated free to beneficiary households.

The CRZ setback line functions as a regulatory restriction on development in the coastal zone, analogous in some respects to a buffer/easement, though it is a regulatory instrument rather than a financial arrangement.

**Coding:** **Community buyout/retreat** (noting this is collective resettlement, not a financial buyout); **Other acquisition tools** (government land provision and allocation). **Leasebacks, easements and buffers** is not coded: the buffer zone is a regulatory setback, not a financial buffer tool.

---

### What legal constraints or requirements were identified during the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Relevant regulations/acts**, **Legal authority over retreat**, **Land acquisition**, **Title(s) transfer**, **Retreat land development**, and **Compliance & enforcement**.

**Narrative:**

- **Relevant regulations/acts:** The primary legal framework was the Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) 1991 Notification issued by the Government of India. Bavinck et al. (2015, p. 596) state: "The main objective of the CRZ 1991 notification was environmental protection," aimed to "restrict industrial and other forms of development in a coastal zone of 500 metres in width." Government Order (GO) 172 (30 March 2005) was issued by the Government of Tamil Nadu, containing guidelines for the relocation of individual dwellings and recommending situating new sites beyond the 500-metre setback line. Observers noted that this interpretation "does not do justice to the refinement of CRZ 1991, and that relocation policy in Tamil Nadu has suffered many ambiguities" (Bavinck et al., 2015, p. 597). In Sri Lanka, a post-tsunami buffer zone policy restricting rebuilding along the coast was the parallel regulatory instrument (Ahmed & McEvoy, 2014, p. 54).

- **Legal authority over retreat:** "District authorities were generally given considerable freedom to decide about relocation" (Bavinck et al., 2015, p. 597, citing personal communication with Vivekanandan). This resulted in different criteria being applied across districts: most sites were situated beyond 500 metres, but in two cases (Koonimedu Kuppam and Mandavai Pudukuppam) a site closer to the shore was approved by district authorities (Bavinck et al., 2015, p. 605).

- **Land acquisition:** Most land was from government reserves; in rare instances, land was procured from private owners (Bavinck et al., 2015, p. 596). In Karikattukuppam, a preferred site belonging to the central Ministry of Tourism was "reluctant to part with the property" and negotiations were prolonged (Bavinck et al., 2015, p. 600).

- **Title(s) transfer:** Bavinck et al. (2015, p. 606) identify this as a significant programmatic innovation: "by allocating individual titles to recipients, it deviated from the tradition of collective property, which prevails especially in rural fishing villages. That men and women are now both included on title deeds is another novelty." In Karikattukuppam, residents were required to relinquish rights to the old site as a condition of receiving keys to new houses (Bavinck et al., 2015, p. 600).

- **Retreat land development:** New settlement design was governed by state guidelines specifying standard house designs. In Sri Lanka, Urban Development Authority guidelines specified land coverage ratios (housing max 65%; common area min 10%; roads, drains etc. min 20%; social infrastructure min 5%) but "did not provide any guidance on the nature and quality of key communal areas" (Ahmed & McEvoy, 2014, p. 56). Little specific site planning guidance was available: "Very little site planning guidelines were available specifically for resettlement programmes; in both the case study countries, general planning guidelines were applied" (Ahmed & McEvoy, 2014, p. 56).

- **Compliance & enforcement:** Bavinck et al. (2015, p. 605) document that "District authorities sometimes have underscored the inevitability of the move by cutting off electricity to the old habitations and transferring food ration cards to the new site" in some instances.

- **Home acquisition:** Not coded. The programme involved building new houses rather than acquiring existing ones from private owners.

- **Litigation:** No formal litigation is documented in the reviewed sources. Community resistance in Chennai evolved from outright resistance to negotiation but did not produce documented formal legal proceedings.

**Coding:** **Relevant regulations/acts** (CRZ 1991, GO 172, Sri Lanka buffer zone policy); **Legal authority over retreat** (delegated to district authorities with inconsistent application); **Land acquisition** (government reserves, some private procurement); **Title(s) transfer** (individual titles allocated as innovation); **Retreat land development** (standard design criteria); **Compliance & enforcement** (electricity cutoffs and ration card transfers in some sites).

---

### What were the funding sources for the MR project? (Local/Municipal only), (Provincial/State only), (Federal only), (Multiple funders), (International aid), (Local/Municipal), (Provincial/State), (Federal), (Individual), (NGOs), (Lenders), (Insurance)

**Answer:** **Multiple funders**: **Provincial/State** (Tamil Nadu government — land and programme coordination); **NGOs** (national and international — construction funding); **International aid** (for Sri Lanka reconstruction). The central Government of India (Federal) set the regulatory framework through CRZ 1991 but is not documented in the sources as a direct construction funder for the Tamil Nadu programme.

**Narrative:** Bavinck et al. (2015, p. 596) describe the Tamil Nadu programme as "a public–private venture, with government seeking the collaboration of NGOs. The general pattern therein seems to have been that the former provided the land…while the latter contributed to the construction process." Different NGOs funded construction at each site (site-specific: MSSS, ECI, World Vision, VCDS, JMM, YMCA Salem, LWS, BGEA, Amma Foundation/Trust, TRC). The Government of Tamil Nadu coordinated the programme and provided land.

For Sri Lanka, Ahmed & McEvoy (2014, p. 54) note: "The large bulk of the post-tsunami reconstruction in Sri Lanka and India was driven by donor agencies that funded the construction of new housing; in this process, the provision of supporting infrastructure was the government's responsibility." Hambantota New Town was built by "various international donor agencies on land donated by the government" (p. 54). Seenigama was implemented "by a local NGO with funding from various international donors" on private land (p. 54). The Ahmed & McEvoy (2014) research was funded by the Australian Research Council (ARC); an earlier related report was AusAID-funded (Shaw and Ahmed, 2010, cited in Ahmed & McEvoy, 2014).

**Coding:** **Multiple funders** — **Provincial/State** (Tamil Nadu government: land provision
